title: Knowing you don't know
hook: to know that you don't know is best (Tao Te Ching 71)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was coarse cloth: the sage in a plain coat with jade held inside. Your line was jade inside.

A meeting. Someone asks a question across the table, and every head turns your way. You half know the answer. Maybe a third. There's a small, fast pressure to fill the silence with something that sounds right. Three short words would end it honestly, and in a room full of waiting faces, they can be hard to say. Chapter seventy-one of the Tao Te Ching is short, and it's built around those words.
screen: `A QUESTION ACROSS THE TABLE.` → `THE PRESSURE TO SOUND RIGHT.` → `THREE HARD WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. To know that you don't know is highest. Not to know, and to think you know, is a sickness. Two kinds of not knowing: one is aware of itself, the other is wearing a costume. Second, the turn. The chapter keeps playing with that word sickness. Only when you treat the sickness as a sickness, it says, are you free of it. The sage isn't sick, because the sage sees the sickness for what it is. Nobody is immune to pretending to know; the sage's health is just catching it. Third, a neighbor. In Plato's Apology, Socrates tells the jury he went around questioning people with a reputation for wisdom, and came away thinking he had one small edge on them: they thought they knew what they didn't, and he didn't think he knew. Two thinkers, far apart, arriving at the same door; neither is borrowing from the other. Fourth, where a real conversation starts. I don't know isn't the end of a conversation. It's where a real one begins. It lets the other person teach you, and it keeps a guess from hardening into a fact that others then build on. It's also a relief: you put down the work of seeming. Chapter seventy-one doesn't praise ignorance. It praises knowing where your knowing stops.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF NOT KNOWING.` · `CALL THE SICKNESS A SICKNESS.` · `SOCRATES LANDS THERE TOO.` · `WHERE A REAL CONVERSATION STARTS.` · then, large: `KNOWING YOU DON'T KNOW.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you've been acting as if you understand: a topic, a person, a decision, maybe something about yourself. Silently, say to it: I don't know, and notice what happens in the body; some tightness may let go, some may grip harder. Stay with the open space those words leave.
Knowing you don't know. Chapter seventy-one: to know that you don't know is highest; to think you know when you don't is a sickness. Today's word.
Your line: I don't know. Three honest words. That's day one thousand one hundred thirty-three.

howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-one as a check on false confidence: being aware of the limits of what you know is counted the healthiest kind of knowing.

Tao Te Ching.meaning: the short Chinese classic of the Way, traditionally credited to Lao-tzu

Socrates.meaning: Greek philosopher of Athens who questioned people about what they knew

Plato.meaning: Greek philosopher, Socrates' student, who wrote the Apology

Apology.meaning: Plato's account of Socrates' defense speech at his trial

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 71 (to know not-knowing is highest; not knowing yet thinking you know is a sickness; the sage treats the sickness as sickness)
Plato, Apology 21d (Socrates on not thinking he knows what he does not know)

notes: Chapter 71 is paraphrased; the writer could not confirm Legge's exact wording. The first line 知不知上 is read here as 'to know that you don't know is highest'; some translators read 'to know, yet think you do not know'. Confirm the reading.
Plato's Apology is paraphrased (no public-domain translation quoted). Reference 21d given from memory; confirm.
The Socrates parallel is presented as a neighbor, with no claim of influence either way.
Trapdoor: 病 (bìng) as the repeated word in chapter 71; confirm.
Original 知不知 (zhī bù zhī) rendered 'JUR boo JUR'. Confirm.
